requests.discriminates: trackingvfs records the path argument verbatim, before delegating, and whatever the inner answers (trackingvfs.go:24-27). Three wrong ports are caught: one that records only successful reads (step 3 reads a path that does not exist and must still be a member -- the package doc names this case exactly, 'including non-existent paths from failed module resolution', trackingvfs.go:1-4); one that normalises, canonicalises or realpaths the key before recording (step 5 reads through '..' and must appear in the set unnormalised, beside the normalised spelling from step 2); and one that folds case before recording on a case-sensitive host (step 7). The inner is mock_over_mapfs, which answers, so each row also pins the forwarded argument and the forwarded answer.

requests.discriminates: FileExists and DirectoryExists are separate tracked methods (trackingvfs.go:29-32 and :50-53), each recording its own argument and each forwarding to its own inner method. The trace asks both about the same three paths, where the two answers disagree, so a port that answers both from one shared stat-derived predicate shows one inner call where the pin shows two of different names. Rust makes that hazard concrete: file_exists and directory_exists are both default trait methods over stat (crates/tsr_vfs/src/lib.rs:77-82), so a wrapper that overrides stat alone inherits both. It also catches result-gated recording -- every one of the six probes is recorded whatever it answered, including the three that answered false -- and a port that records a path's parent directory as well, which seen_size would expose.

It also catches a port that resolves first and records afterwards, and one that declines to record when the inner leaves the path unchanged (step 3 asks about a path that does not exist, where iovfs.Realpath returns the input verbatim, iofs.go:190-199).

requests.discriminates: The plan's lost-timestamp-arguments control on the tracking adapter. The two instants differ and are deliberately non-chronological, so a port that drops aTime, passes mTime in both positions, or swaps them is caught by the ordered inner call at step 2, which carries both arguments. A correction to the survey draft: the store cannot witness aTime at all, because the pinned vfstest MapFS.Chtimes assigns only `fileInfo.ModTime = mTime` (vfstest.go:605-617), so the forwarded call is the only place both instants are visible and step 3 pins which one reached the store. Chtimes is also a write-class method and is untracked (trackingvfs.go:46-48), so steps 2 and 5 must leave SeenFiles alone. Rust has no expression for this at all: change_times(&self, _path) takes no instants (crates/tsr_vfs/src/lib.rs:92-94).

requests.discriminates: The forwarded capability failure. Over an inner that is an io/fs without iovfs.WritableFS, all four write-class methods panic from iovfs's own unsupported stubs (iofs.go:91-103) with literal pinned text, and the tracking wrapper adds nothing: it neither recovers them, nor records anything, nor answers in the inner's place. Step 7 shows the store is untouched.

requests.discriminates: The plan's swapped-walk-callback control. WalkDir records the root and then hands the inner its OWN closure, which records each arriving path before calling the caller's walkFn (trackingvfs.go:65-71). A port that passes the caller's walkFn straight through leaves SeenFiles holding only the root, which this trace makes unmissable: the set must hold the root and all five descendants. It is also the deliberate contrast with GetAccessibleEntries, which records its argument and nothing it listed. There is no Rust expression yet -- the trait has no walk_dir (crates/tsr_vfs/src/lib.rs:70-95) -- so there is no callback to wrap.

requests.discriminates: The recording happens BEFORE the caller's walkFn runs (trackingvfs.go:67-69), so a directory the caller skips is still a dependency and is still recorded. A port that records after walkFn returns, or that declines to record when the callback returns a sentinel, loses '/root/sub' from the set. A port that records the skipped directory's children as well is caught in the other direction: '/root/sub/b.ts' and '/root/sub/deep/c.ts' were never visited and must not be members. '/root/z.ts' is in the tree so that the sentinel itself is pinned rather than merely 'some early stop': SkipDir returned from a directory is nilled by io/fs walk.go:73-78 and the walk resumes at the following sibling, so '/root/z.ts' must arrive fourth -- where a port that mapped SkipDir onto SkipAll would end the walk at three (walk.go:124-126 absorbs both sentinels, so the returned error class cannot tell them apart and only the extra arrival can).
requests.subject: trackingvfs.FS

requests.discriminates: The two early stops that io/fs treats differently from SkipDir, on one tree, each with a fresh tracker so the sets do not blend. SkipAll is absorbed by fs.WalkDir and the walk returns nil; a callback error is not and reaches the caller. Both leave the terminating path in SeenFiles, because trackingvfs records before it calls walkFn (trackingvfs.go:67-69). The stop points are chosen so the sentinel is load-bearing rather than incidental: '/root/sub/b.ts' is below the walk root and has a following uncle in '/root/z.ts', so SkipAll ends the walk after four arrivals where SkipDir would break out of '/root/sub' only (io/fs walk.go:73-78 leaves SkipDir unnilled on a non-directory and walk.go:96-97 breaks the parent loop) and resume at '/root/z.ts' for a fifth. A port that treats any non-nil callback return as 'do not record' fails both walks; a port that maps SkipAll onto SkipDir arrives at '/root/z.ts' and records a fifth member at step 2, which is the only signal there is, since walk.go:124-126 absorbs both sentinels into a nil walk error; a port that swallows the callback's own error reports an empty walk error class at step 4, where the pin propagates it and does not resume at '/root/z.ts' either.

requests.discriminates: Wrap with an empty Replacements is a pure passthrough, and this is the forwarding trace for all twelve methods: each is called exactly once, in the order the interface declares them, and each row must show exactly one inner call of the matching name with the arguments verbatim. The inner is mock_over_mapfs with no silent methods, so it answers everything and a missing forward would be visible as an empty inner log rather than as a panic. It catches a port that routes several methods through one -- file_exists and directory_exists through stat, which is what the Rust trait's defaults do (crates/tsr_vfs/src/lib.rs:77-82); append through read plus write; entries through a walk -- and a port that answers anything from a cache instead of the inner.

requests.discriminates: The most plausible misreading of 'wrap' is consulting the inner first and using the replacement only when the inner returns a zero value or an error. The pin does the opposite: an installed replacement answers and the inner is not consulted at all (wrapvfs.go:125-130). The inner's Realpath Func is deliberately left nil here, so any forwarding panics with the generated mock's own sentence rather than quietly producing the right answer -- the case proves a call was NOT forwarded rather than just that the answer came from elsewhere. Steps 4 and 5 catch the other misreading, a port that treats a Realpath replacement as a path-mapping layer applied to every method. That is the exact production shape: the pin's only wrapvfs caller replaces Realpath alone for module resolution (tsc/internal/ls/autoimport/util.go:319), where rewriting the other methods' arguments would be wrong.
requests.subject: wrapvfs.Wrap

requests.discriminates: Wrap copies Replacements into wrappedFS (wrapvfs.go:24-29), so editing the caller's own table afterwards cannot reach the wrapper. Step 3 rewrites exactly the Realpath field of the same variable that was handed to Wrap -- it mutates in place rather than rebinding -- so a port that stored a pointer, an Rc or any live reference answers '/second' at step 4 where the pin still answers '/first'. The inner's Realpath Func is nil, so a port that instead dropped the replacement entirely is distinguished too: it would panic rather than answer either string.

requests.discriminates: The representation hazard worth freezing. Go's ReadFile contract is an independent pair (contents string, ok bool) (vfs.go:19-21), so ("", true) and ("X", false) are both legal and distinct, and the wrapper returns the replacement's pair verbatim (wrapvfs.go:53-58). Rust's read_file returns Result<Option<FileContent>, Error> (crates/tsr_vfs/src/lib.rs:73), which cannot express ("X", false) at all and collapses ("", true) and a miss onto neighbouring shapes. It also catches a port that falls back to the inner when ok is false or the contents are empty: the inner's ReadFile Func is nil, so any forwarding panics instead of answering.
